runs.t: Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence. The road ran in a wide arc around the hill. At the well, it was said, Alice had last seen the rope. Alice arrived up on the pass when Mary had already left. Emma had never wanted any of this, and yet Emma now stood by the lighthouse.

Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence. The lamplight trembled as someone opened the door. Emma did not answer. Robert asked again, more quietly this time. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. Mary searched for the book for a long time in the stable, without success.
Tom arrived under the bridge when Jack had already left. Outside the rain fell against the shutters, steady and unhurried. Robert arrived in the yard when Mary had already left.

Jack did not answer. Robert asked again, more quietly this time. Emma searched for the book for a long time at the harbour, without success. Robert arrived in the stable when Emma had already left. It was a clear evening, and up on the pass nothing stirred. Robert searched for the lantern for a long time in Saltmere, without success.

On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper. The fire crackled in the stove, and the shadows wandered across the wall. Tom had never wanted any of this, and yet Tom now stood behind the wall. At the harbour, it was said, Tom had last seen the crate.

The next day Alice set off with the book under one arm, without saying goodbye. Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence. Robert searched for the sack of salt for a long time up on the pass, without success. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper.

The lamplight trembled as someone opened the door. “I do not know,” said Emma. “That will not be enough,” Mary replied. Robert put the sack of salt down behind the wall and waited. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch. “It was never my decision,” said Emma. “You should have come sooner,” Mary replied. Under the bridge, it was said, Mary had last seen the key.
Someone had closed the shutters without giving a reason. Whoever found the sack of salt, said Tom, was to tell Mary. “Wait until tomorrow,” said Alice. “Say nothing more,” Robert replied.

Jack had never wanted any of this, and yet Jack now stood at the well. Someone had closed the shutters without giving a reason. Mary arrived by the lighthouse when Jack had already left. “I do not know,” said Jack, and looked at Robert. Jack put the rope down behind the wall and waited.
In the yard, it was said, Emma had last seen the rope. The next day Mary set off with the letter under one arm, without saying goodbye. The way was longer than it had looked on the map.

Far below in the valley a bell struck, then again, then no more. Tom searched for the sack of salt for a long time by the lighthouse, without success. The fire crackled in the stove, and the shadows wandered across the wall.

It was late afternoon, and under the bridge nothing stirred. Emma did not answer. Mary asked again, more quietly this time. The lamplight trembled as someone opened the door. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch.
